title: Embroidery Stitches (Module 6B, lesson 31)
summary: Wash and wipe your hands before starting. If the thread twists or knots, turn the needle in the opposite direction or use a fresh length. Always start an embroidery with a back stitch and never with a knot. Back stitch is a very strong stitch, worked from right to left on the wrong side: insert the needle where the embroidery begins, pick a few threads and pull through; repeat picking a few extra threads. Buy all threads beforehand because a slight change of shade can spoil the effect.

Stem stitch: an outline stitch giving a fine line, used for edges, stems and veins; the needle is inserted to the right of the line and brought up to the left; rows alongside can fill. Satin stitch: a filling stitch giving a very smooth finish; straight stitches worked slantwise with equal thread at front and back (straight areas slantwise from top to bottom; small circle long stitches centre first; leaf diagonally from the left edge). Long and short stitch: fills areas in solid and shaded colours; the first row has alternating long and short stitches and following rows have equal-length stitches. Chain stitch: appears like a chain on the face; worked from the top down by holding the loop with the thumb and inserting the needle at the same point; used for heavy outlines or as filling. Darning stitch: a filling stitch visible only on the face of the fabric, with floats only in front (unlike satin stitch with equal floats on both sides). Herringbone stitch (Machali Tanka): worked between two lines with short stitches alternately in the upper and lower line, interlacing; used for thick seams or to connect solid areas. Buttonhole stitch: worked from left to right, with the thread held under the left thumb to form a loop, stitches very close together; for filling or finishing edges, especially in patchwork. Blanket stitch: like buttonhole but with the stitches a little distance apart; used for edges of blankets and carpets. Cross stitch: forms X's on the face; worked in two journeys with the needle pointing left (top to bottom, then bottom to top) so thread floats cross in the middle. French knot: bring the thread up, wrap it over and under the needle, and insert the needle close to where it came up; double thread for larger knots.

Do not end in a big knot and keep the back as neat as the front; clip extra threads at the back; wash or dry clean the article after embroidery; starch and iron well; finish the edges by hemming or picoting; fold heavily embroidered articles in mulmul cloth for storage. Careful selection of design, embroidery stitch and colour gives striking results.

objective: Read the descriptions. (i) A filling stitch where the thread is visible only on the face of the fabric, creating floats only on the front side. (ii) A stitch worked between two lines with interlocking diagonal threads, often used for thick seams or connecting areas. Identify the stitches. Options: (a) Darning stitch (b) Herringbone stitch (c) Blanket stitch (d) Long and short stitch.

Rahul is embroidering a garment. Part A: Which of the following is not part of darning stitch? (i) It is a filling stitch (ii) The stitch is visible only on the face of the fabric (iii) The front has floats (iv) The thread floats cross in the middle forming an X. Part B: Which stitch should he use for finishing edges in a patchwork?
Part A: (iv), because that describes cross stitch. Part B: buttonhole stitch.
State True or False. (a) A knot may be used to start the embroidery. (b) The back of the embroidery should be as neat as the front.
(a) False: start with a back stitch. (b) True.
Match Column A with Column B. A: (a) Satin stitch (b) Stem stitch. B: (i) Outline stitch (ii) Smooth filling stitch (iii) Loops on the surface.
vsa: Why is it recommended to avoid using a knot at the start of embroidery work? What is the correct way to begin instead?
A knot makes a lump and shows on the front and can come undone. Begin with a back stitch, which is strong and neat.
What is the difference between buttonhole stitch and blanket stitch?
Both are looped edge stitches. In buttonhole stitch the stitches are very close together; in blanket stitch they are a little distance apart.
Satin stitch and long and short stitch (also darning stitch).
It is used for heavy outlines, or in rows following the outline as a filling.
State two points about the finishing of an embroidered article.
Clip the extra threads at the back and wash or dry clean the article. Starch and iron it well and finish the edges by hemming or picoting.
sa: Write the steps of making a satin stitch and a French knot stitch.

(i) Satin stitch: work straight stitches slantwise, taking the thread out equally at the front and back so that the surface is smooth, e.g. from top to bottom for straight areas. (ii) French knot: bring the thread up through the fabric and wrap it over and under the needle. (iii) Then insert the needle into the fabric close to where it came up; use double thread for a larger knot.
Uma is embroidering a baby blanket with multicoloured butterflies. Suggest two stitches to fill the motif and one for the edge, with reasons.
(i) Satin stitch gives a smooth filling for wings. (ii) Long and short stitch fills shaded colours. (iii) Blanket stitch for the edge because it is the traditional finish for blankets.
Explain the steps of back stitch (three points).

(i) Thread the needle and insert it where the embroidery begins. (ii) Pick a few threads of the fabric and pull the needle and thread through. (iii) Repeat at the same place picking a few extra threads; it is worked on the wrong side from right to left.
Explain how the finishing of an embroidered article is done (three points).
(i) Do not end in a big knot; keep the back neat and clip extra threads. (ii) Wash or dry clean, starch and iron it. (iii) Finish the edges by hemming or picoting and store in mulmul cloth.
la: Describe the ten basic embroidery stitches briefly.

(i) Stem stitch is an outline stitch and satin stitch a smooth filling. (ii) Long and short stitch fills shaded areas and chain stitch makes loops for outlines. (iii) Darning stitch has floats only on the face. (iv) Herringbone stitch is worked between two lines. (v) Buttonhole stitch has close stitches and blanket stitch has spaced stitches for edges. (vi) Cross stitch forms X's and French knot is a wrapped knot.
